claims.text: A Mg-based alloy containing Ti, Zr, and Mn can remain below 6 g/cm³.
Sintering at 850–900 °C with rapid thermal cycling can produce a dense, single-phase-like microstructure.
Rapid thermal cycling suppresses element segregation and volatile loss.
The initial high-surface-area Mg-transition-metal powder mixture is prone to segregation and volatile loss during standard sintering.
Heating above 50 °C/min and cooling above 100 °C/min minimize dwell time at peak temperature and balance densification against volatility and phase instability.
An inert Ar atmosphere prevents oxidation during processing.
Spark plasma sintering can enhance densification at lower temperatures.
Multicomponent transition-metal additions induce sluggish diffusion kinetics in the proposed Mg-based alloy.
Sluggish diffusion stabilizes a single-phase solid solution and suppresses TCP-phase formation.
Rapid thermal cycling prevents grain coarsening and element segregation.
The 850–900 °C window avoids the Mg volatility threshold, which is above 900 °C.
Temperatures of 850–900 °C provide sufficient thermal energy for diffusion-driven homogenization.
Limiting time at temperature suppresses phase separation and Mg loss and thereby promotes a metastable single-phase-like microstructure.
The proposed process will yield relative density above 95% with minimal porosity.
The resulting microstructure will be a single-phase-like FCC or BCC solid solution.
A uniform protective surface oxide improves oxidation and corrosion resistance.
The protective surface layer will comprise an MgO/TiO2/ZrO2 composite.
Standard sintering at 950–1000 °C causes Mg volatility, segregation, multiphase microstructures, pore formation, reduced density, and poor barrier properties.
Below 800 °C, insufficient diffusion causes relative density to fall below 90%.
Above 950 °C, Mg loss exceeds 5% and causes porosity and microstructural instability.

contradictions.description: The mechanism places the Mg volatility threshold above 900 °C, whereas the boundary states that volatility dominates only above 950 °C; the 900–950 °C interval is therefore inconsistently classified.
The target is described as single-phase-like, but the phase is left as either FCC or BCC without specifying which structure is expected for the proposed Mg-transition-metal system.
